data.title: Yellow nail syndrome — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Yellow nail syndrome** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Write a note on yellow nail syndrome (PYQ).**
- Rare disorder with the triad: yellow slow-growing nails, lymphoedema (usually lower limbs) and respiratory involvement (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, recurrent bronchitis/pneumonia) — two of three features enough for diagnosis
- Adults (median ~50 y); impaired lymphatic drainage (functional lymphatic abnormality) with microvasculopathy

**Q2. Describe the nail changes.**
- Diffusely yellow to yellow-green thickened nails, increased transverse and longitudinal curvature (overcurved), loss of cuticle, absent lunula, onycholysis, very slow growth (<0.25 mm/week; normal ~0.5–1.2 mm), onychomadesis; all 20 nails often affected

**Q3. Associations.**
- Malignancies (lung, breast, lymphoma), autoimmune disease (RA, thyroid), immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, AIDS, drugs (penicillamine, bucillamine, gold, titanium dental implants/joint prostheses — titanium exposure hypothesis)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of yellow nails.**
- Onychomycosis (KOH/culture), psoriasis, ageing, nicotine staining (proximal spared), carotenaemia (skin also yellow), tetracycline/ antimalarial pigmentation, jaundice (sclera), pachyonychia congenita, nail varnish staining, diabetes (yellowish nails)

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Chest X-ray/HRCT, pleural fluid analysis (exudative, lymphocytic, sometimes chylous), sinus imaging, lymphoscintigraphy, nail clipping KOH/culture, screen for associated malignancy/autoimmunity

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Nails: oral vitamin E (α-tocopherol 800–1200 IU/day) ± oral itraconazole/fluconazole pulse (increase nail growth), zinc, topical vitamin E; nails may improve spontaneously (~30%)
- Lymphoedema: compression, physiotherapy, skin care
- Respiratory: pleurodesis/decortication for recurrent effusions, antibiotics and physiotherapy for bronchiectasis; octreotide (chylous effusions)
- Remove titanium implants if implicated

**Q7. Describe the anatomy and growth of the nail unit (linked PYQ).**
- Components: nail plate (keratin — hard keratins), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium), lateral folds, matrix (proximal — dorsal plate; distal — ventral plate; lunula is visible distal matrix), nail bed, hyponychium
- Growth: fingernail ~3 mm/month (complete regrowth 4–6 months), toenail ~1 mm/month (12–18 months); faster in summer, dominant hand, pregnancy, psoriasis; slower in elderly, illness, yellow nail syndrome

**Q8. Associations in detail.**
- Primary/ idiopathic; secondary — malignancies (lymphoma, breast, lung), immunodeficiencies, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, nephrotic syndrome, drugs (penicillamine, gold, bucillamine, titanium implants — 'titanium yellow nail')

**Q9. Treatment in detail.**
- Nails: oral vitamin E 1000–1200 IU/day, oral itraconazole/ fluconazole pulse therapy (stimulate growth), zinc; topical vitamin E; nails may improve spontaneously (~30%)
- Lymphoedema: compression, physiotherapy
- Pleural effusion: thoracentesis, pleurodesis, octreotide (chylous)
- Sinusitis/ bronchiectasis: antibiotics, physiotherapy
- Remove titanium implants if implicated

**Q10. Differential diagnosis of yellow nails in detail.**
- Onychomycosis (subungual debris, KOH +), psoriasis, ageing, smoking (nicotine stain), nail polish staining, carotenaemia, jaundice, tetracyclines, diabetes (glycation), lymphoedema-associated nail changes, PXE

**Q11. What is the prognosis?**
- Chronic disease; nail changes may remit in ~1/3; respiratory complications determine morbidity; life expectancy mildly reduced in some series

**Q12. Investigations in detail.**
- Chest X-ray/ CT (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis), pleural fluid analysis (exudate, lymphocyte-rich, sometimes chylous), sinus imaging, lymphoscintigraphy (lymphatic hypoplasia), nail KOH/ culture to exclude onychomycosis, screen for malignancy/ autoimmune disease/ thyroid, review titanium exposure

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Functional/ anatomical lymphatic abnormality (lymphatic hypoplasia or impaired drainage) leading to slow nail growth (<0.25 mm/week) and thickened, discoloured nails, pleural effusions and lymphoedema; may be primary or secondary

**Q14. Classic triad and its frequency.**
- Yellow nails + lymphoedema (usually lower limbs) + respiratory involvement (pleural effusion — chylous/exudative, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonia); full triad in only about one-third; two of three are enough for diagnosis

**Q15. Nail findings in detail.**
- Thick, hard, yellow to green, excessively curved transversely and longitudinally, loss of cuticle, onycholysis, very slow growth, absence of lunulae; all 20 nails often affected

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow overcurved slow-growing nails + lymphoedema + pleural effusion — yellow nail syndrome
- Vitamin E + itraconazole

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nail disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
